column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: The seventh day of the week (from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset), kept holy as a day of rest and worship. God rested on the seventh day of creation, and the Sabbath was a sign of his covenant with Israel. No work was done; in Jesus' day people met in the synagogue to hear the Scriptures read. Jesus called himself Lord of the Sabbath, and Christians have kept the first day, the day of his resurrection, as the Lord's Day.

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: The spring feast remembering the night God freed Israel from Egypt: the angel of death "passed over" the houses marked with a lamb's blood. Each family ate a roast lamb with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, on the evening of the 14th of Nisan (March or April). Jesus was crucified at Passover; the New Testament calls him "Christ our Passover" (1 Cor 5:7), and the Lord's Supper began at a Passover meal.

column4: feast of unleavened bread|festival of unleavened bread|days of unleavened bread|unleavened bread
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: Seven days straight after Passover when no bread with yeast (leaven) was eaten, and all leaven was cleared from the house. It recalled the haste of leaving Egypt, with no time for dough to rise. Paul uses it as a picture of a life cleared of malice and wickedness (1 Cor 5:7-8).

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: The first and best of the harvest, given to God before the rest was used, as thanks that all of it came from him. A sheaf of the first barley was waved before the Lord the day after the Sabbath of Passover week. Paul calls the risen Christ "the firstfruits of them that slept" (1 Cor 15:20): the first of the great harvest of the resurrection.

column4: pentecost|feast of weeks|festival of weeks|feast of harvest|festival of harvest|harvest festival
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: The harvest feast held fifty days (seven weeks) after Passover, when two loaves from the new wheat were offered. "Pentecost" is Greek for "fiftieth". Jews from many lands came to Jerusalem for it, which is why so many nations heard the apostles when the Holy Spirit was poured out at Pentecost (Acts 2).

column4: feast of trumpets|festival of trumpets|blowing of trumpets|blowing of the trumpets|day of blowing|day for you to blow the trumpets|trumpet blasts
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: A holy day of rest on the first day of the seventh month (September or October), announced by the blowing of trumpets (the ram's horn). It began the most solemn month of Israel's year, leading to the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Tabernacles. In later Judaism it became the New Year (Rosh Hashanah).

column4: day of atonement|day of the atonement|day of atonements|atonement day
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: The holiest day of Israel's year (Yom Kippur), on the tenth day of the seventh month: a day of fasting and confession. Only on this day did the high priest enter the Most Holy Place, with the blood of a sacrifice, to make atonement for the sins of the whole nation; a second goat, the scapegoat, carried their sins away into the wilderness. Hebrews shows Jesus as the great High Priest who entered heaven itself with his own blood, once for all.

column4: feast of tabernacles|feast of the tabernacles|feast of booths|festival of booths|festival of shelters|feast of shelters|feast of ingathering|festival of ingathering
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: The joyful autumn feast at the end of harvest, from the 15th of the seventh month for seven days. Families lived in shelters (booths) made of branches, to remember Israel's tents in the wilderness. Water was poured out at the temple each day and great lamps were lit; on the last day Jesus stood and offered "living water" (John 7:37-38).

column4: new moon|new moons|new moon's|new moon festival|new moon festivals|new moon feast|new moon feasts|new moon celebrations|beginnings of your months|beginning of your months
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: The first day of each month in Israel's calendar, which followed the moon. Trumpets were blown, extra offerings made and work often stopped, with family meals (1 Sam 20). Paul says such days were "a shadow of things to come", while the reality is Christ (Col 2:16-17).

column4: appointed feasts|appointed feast|appointed festivals|appointed festival|solemn feasts|solemn feast|set feasts|appointed times|feasts of the lord|festivals of the lord|appointed seasons
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: The holy days God gave Israel (Lev 23): the weekly Sabbath, and the yearly feasts of Passover and Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Weeks (Pentecost), Trumpets, the Day of Atonement and Tabernacles. Three times a year, at Unleavened Bread, Weeks and Tabernacles, every man was to appear before the Lord at his sanctuary. They marked Israel's year with God's saving acts and the harvests he gave.

column4: seventh year|year of release|release|sabbath of rest|year of rest|rest for the land|the land shall keep a sabbath|cancel debts|cancellation of debts|cancel the debts
column10: Every seventh year the fields were left unsown so the land could rest, and what grew by itself was left for the poor and the animals. Debts between Israelites were cancelled, and Hebrew servants were set free. It taught that the land was the Lord's; the exile's seventy years were linked to the Sabbath years Israel had not kept (2 Chr 36:21).

column4: jubilee|jubile|year of jubilee|year of jubile|the jubilee year
column10: Every fiftieth year, after seven Sabbath years, a trumpet on the Day of Atonement proclaimed liberty through the land. Land that had been sold went back to the family it was first given to, and Israelites who had sold themselves as servants went free. Jesus read Isaiah's "acceptable year of the Lord", which echoes the Jubilee, as fulfilled in himself (Luke 4:18-21).

A joyful feast on the 14th and 15th of the month Adar (February or March), remembering how God saved the Jews in Persia from Haman's plot, as told in Esther. "Pur" means "lot": Haman cast lots to choose the day to destroy them. It was kept with feasting, gifts to one another and gifts to the poor.

column4: feast of the dedication|feast of dedication|festival of dedication|festival of the dedication|hanukkah
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: A winter feast of eight days (in December), remembering the cleansing and rededication of the temple in 164 BC, after the Maccabees freed it from the Greek king Antiochus, who had defiled it. It was also called the Feast of Lights, as lamps were lit in every home. Jesus was in the temple at this feast when he said, "I and my Father are one" (John 10:30).

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: Going without food for a time, to humble oneself before God: in sorrow for sin, in grief, or when seeking God's help. The Law commanded only one fast, on the Day of Atonement ("the fast" of Acts 27:9); others were added for times of trouble. Pharisees fasted twice a week; Jesus taught that fasting should be done for God's eyes, not to be seen.

column4: preparation|day of preparation|preparation day|day before the sabbath
column10: The day before the Sabbath (Friday), when food was cooked and everything readied so no work need be done on the Sabbath. Jesus died on a preparation day; his body had to be buried before sunset, when the Sabbath began.

column4: sabbath day's journey|sabbath day journey|sabbath day's walk|sabbath day walk
column10: The distance the rabbis allowed a person to walk on the Sabbath: about 2,000 cubits, roughly two-thirds of a mile (1 km). Acts uses it to say how near the Mount of Olives was to Jerusalem.

column4: third hour|sixth hour|ninth hour|seventh hour|tenth hour|eleventh hour|first hour|hour of prayer
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: In Jesus' day the daylight was counted in twelve hours from sunrise (about 6 a.m.). The third hour was about 9 a.m., the sixth about noon and the ninth about 3 p.m.; the morning and evening sacrifices at the temple were the usual hours of prayer. John's Gospel may count from midnight, as the Romans did.

column4: watch|watches|morning watch|middle watch|fourth watch|second watch|third watch
column10: The night was divided into watches, the times when guards took turns. The Old Testament counts three watches; in Roman times there were four, of three hours each, from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. Jesus walked on the water "in the fourth watch", just before dawn.

column4: hear o israel|listen o israel|hear israel|listen israel
column9: Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God is one Lord (Deut 6:4), the confession of faith every Jew said morning and evening, named from its first word in Hebrew, "Shema" ("Hear"). Jesus quoted it as the first and greatest commandment, with the call to love God with all your heart, soul, mind and strength.

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: The strictest religious party among the Jews, known for careful keeping of the Law and of the "tradition of the elders" added to it, especially on the Sabbath, tithing and ritual washing. They believed in the resurrection and in angels. Many opposed Jesus, who rebuked their hypocrisy, but some, like Nicodemus and Paul, came to believe.

A party of wealthy, priestly families who controlled the temple and much of the council. They accepted only the written Law and denied the resurrection, angels and spirits. They worked with Rome to keep their power, and led the opposition to the apostles' preaching of Jesus' resurrection.

column4: scribe|scribes|teacher of the law|teachers of the law|teachers of religious law|teacher of religious law|experts in the law|expert in the law|lawyer|lawyers|doctors of the law|doctor of the law|teachers of the scriptures
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: Experts who copied, studied and taught the Law of Moses and how it applied to daily life. Ezra was the great scribe after the exile. In Jesus' day most scribes were Pharisees and sat on the council; people were amazed that Jesus taught "as one having authority, and not as the scribes" (Matt 7:29). In the early kingdom a "scribe" was a royal secretary.

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: The highest Jewish court in Jerusalem, of 71 members: chief priests, elders and scribes, led by the high priest. Under Rome it governed religious matters but could not carry out a death sentence, which is why Jesus was handed to Pilate. Peter, John, Stephen and Paul were all tried before it.

Jews who supported the rule of Herod's family, and so Rome. Though usually opposed to the Pharisees, they joined them in plotting against Jesus and in trying to trap him with the question of paying taxes to Caesar.

Jews zealous to free their nation from Rome, some by violence. One of the twelve apostles, Simon, was called the Zealot ("Canaanite" in the King James Version comes from the Aramaic word for "zealous", not the land of Canaan).

The people of Samaria, between Judea and Galilee, descended from Israelites left after the Assyrian conquest and foreigners settled there. They worshipped on Mount Gerizim and accepted only the five books of Moses. Jews and Samaritans despised each other, which is why Jesus' talk with the Samaritan woman and his parable of the Good Samaritan were so startling.

column4: publican|publicans|tax collector|tax collectors|tax-collector|tax-collectors|chief tax collector|chief among the publicans|collector of taxes
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: Jews who collected taxes for Rome, often taking more than was owed and keeping the rest. They were hated as traitors and cheats, and ranked with "sinners". Jesus ate with them and called one, Matthew, to be an apostle; Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, repaid four times what he had taken.

All peoples who were not Jews. Jews kept apart from them, would not eat with them, and kept them out of the inner temple courts. Yet God promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed through him; the New Testament tells how the gospel went to the Gentiles and made Jew and Gentile one in Christ.

column4: proselyte|proselytes|converts to judaism|convert to judaism|converts|proselyte to judaism
column10: Gentiles who became Jews, accepting circumcision and the whole Law. Many others, called "God-fearers" or "devout" (like Cornelius), worshipped Israel's God without fully converting; many of the first Gentile believers came from among them.

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: Rabbi means "my master" or "my teacher": a respectful title for a teacher of the Law, who gathered disciples to learn from him and live with him. Jesus was called Rabbi; Mary Magdalene called him "Rabboni" at the tomb.

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: A disciple was a learner who followed a teacher, lived with him and copied his way of life. John the Baptist and the Pharisees had disciples; Jesus called many to follow him and chose twelve as apostles. Jesus told his followers to make disciples of all nations.
The founding fathers of Israel: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Jacob's twelve sons, the heads of the tribes. The New Testament also calls David and Abraham patriarchs.

column4: twelve tribes|tribes of israel|twelve tribes of israel|tribe|tribes
column10: Israel was made up of twelve tribes, each descended from one of Jacob's sons (with Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, counted as tribes and Levi given no land). Each tribe received its own share of the land. Jesus promised the apostles they would sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes.

column4: betroth|betrothed|betrothest|espoused|espouse|pledged to be married|pledged to marry|engaged|promised in marriage|promised to be married|to be married
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: Betrothal was the binding first stage of marriage, made by agreement between families, often with a bride price, about a year before the wedding. The couple were legally husband and wife, though they did not yet live together; ending it needed a divorce. That is why Joseph, betrothed to Mary, planned to "put her away privately" (Matt 1:19).

column4: wedding|weddings|marriage feast|wedding feast|wedding banquet|wedding garment|wedding clothes|wedding hall|wedding guests|bridechamber|bride chamber|children of the bridechamber|friend of the bridegroom
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: At the wedding the bridegroom came with his friends, often at night with lamps, to bring the bride to his home, where a feast lasted up to a week. Guests wore festive clothes, and running out of wine was a real shame for the family (John 2). Jesus' parables of the wedding feast and the ten virgins draw on these customs.

column4: dowry|bride price|bride-price|marriage present|mohar|price for the bride|endowment
column10: A payment or service the bridegroom gave the bride's family at betrothal. Jacob worked seven years for Rachel; Saul asked David for a hundred Philistine foreskins, hoping he would be killed.

column4: brother|brother's|husband's brother|brother's wife|raise up seed|raise up offspring|raise up children|perform the duty
column10: If a man died without a son, his brother was to marry the widow, and their first son would carry on the dead man's name and inherit his land. A brother who refused was shamed at the city gate. The Sadducees used this law to try to trap Jesus with a question about the resurrection.

column4: kinsman|kinsmen|near kinsman|next of kin|near relative|close relative|relative|guardian-redeemer|guardian redeemer|family redeemer|redeemer|redeem|redemption|one of our redeemers
column10: The nearest male relative (Hebrew "goel") had the right and duty to help a family member in trouble: to buy back land that had been sold, to free a relative sold into slavery, and to carry on a dead man's name. Boaz did this for Ruth and Naomi. God calls himself Israel's Redeemer, and Christians have long seen Christ in the kinsman who pays the price to set his people free.

column4: avenger of blood|revenger of blood|avenger|revenger|city of refuge|cities of refuge
column10: In Israel the nearest relative of a person killed was to avenge them. To protect someone who killed by accident, God appointed six cities of refuge; the killer could flee there and be safe until a fair trial, and could go home free when the high priest died.

column4: glean|gleaned|gleaning|gleanings|gleaneth|glean among the sheaves|corners of your field|corners of thy field|edges of your field
column10: Farmers were not to reap the edges of their fields, gather what fell, or strip their vines and olive trees bare: what was left was for the poor, the widow, the orphan and the foreigner to gather. This is how Ruth, a poor widow from Moab, came to glean in Boaz's field.

A flat, hard area of earth or rock, often on a hill to catch the wind, where harvested grain was beaten or trampled by oxen to loosen the kernels. Then it was winnowed. Men slept there at harvest to guard the grain, as Boaz did. David bought Araunah's threshing floor, where Solomon later built the temple.

After threshing, the grain and straw were tossed into the air with a fork or shovel (the KJV "fan"); the wind blew the light chaff away and the heavy grain fell back. John the Baptist used it as a picture of Christ's judgment, separating the wheat from the chaff.

column4: gate|gates|gate of the city|city gate|gate of his city|gates of the city|town gate
column10: The gateway of a walled town was its centre of public life: the elders sat there to judge cases and witness agreements, business was done, and news was shared. Boaz settled his right to marry Ruth before ten elders at the gate; the good wife's husband is "known in the gates" (Prov 31:23).

column4: elder|elders|elders of israel|elders of the people|elders of the city|elders of the town
column10: Older men who led their families, towns and the nation, judged cases and represented the people. In Jesus' day the elders were part of the council with the chief priests and scribes. In the church, elders (also called overseers) were appointed to lead and care for each congregation.

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: Welcoming travellers and strangers was a sacred duty in the Bible's world, where there were few inns. A host gave water to wash the feet, food, and shelter, and protected the guest. Abraham welcomed three visitors who turned out to be the Lord and angels; Hebrews remembers it: "some have entertained angels unawares".

column4: wash|washed|washing|washeth|feet|wash his feet|wash your feet|washed his feet|washed their feet|wash the feet|washing of feet
column10: People walked dusty roads in sandals, so a host offered water to wash a guest's feet, and the lowest servant did the washing. When Jesus, their Lord and Teacher, washed his disciples' feet, he gave them an example of humble service.

column4: reclined|reclining|recline|sat at meat|sat at table|sitting at meat|lay|leaning|lying|leaned|sat down|at table|reclined at table
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: At feasts in Jesus' day guests lay on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow with their feet stretched out behind. That is how a woman could come behind Jesus and wash his feet, and how John could lean back against Jesus at the Last Supper. The places nearest the host were the places of honour.

column4: covenant|cut a covenant|made a covenant|pieces|between the pieces|divided them|cut in two|heap|pillar|witness
column10: A covenant was a solemn binding agreement. It was often sealed by cutting animals in two and walking between the pieces, as if to say, "may this happen to me if I break it"; or by a shared meal, a heap of stones or a pillar as witness. In Genesis 15 God alone passed between the pieces, binding himself to keep his promise to Abraham.

A solemn promise calling on God as witness. Some were made by putting a hand under the other's thigh. Jesus taught his followers to be so truthful that a plain "yes" or "no" is enough, rather than piling up oaths.

column4: lot|lots|cast lots|casting lots|the lot fell|cast the lot
column10: Marked stones or sticks drawn or thrown to make a decision, trusting God to decide: "the lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the Lord" (Prov 16:33). The land was divided by lot, priests' duties were chosen by lot, and the apostles chose Matthias so. The soldiers cast lots for Jesus' clothes, as Psalm 22 had said.

column4: birthright|birth right|rights as the firstborn|rights of the firstborn|right of the firstborn|firstborn's right
column10: The special rights of the firstborn son: a double share of the inheritance and leadership of the family after the father. Esau sold his birthright to Jacob for a meal; Hebrews warns against treating holy things as lightly as he did.

Near death, a father solemnly blessed his sons, speaking God's promises over their future. Once given, the blessing could not be taken back, which is why Esau wept bitterly when Jacob received it by a trick.

In the ancient world many people were servants or slaves, through debt, war or birth. The Law limited it among Israelites: a Hebrew servant went free in the seventh year, and was not to be ruled harshly, for Israel had been slaves in Egypt. The New Testament calls masters to treat slaves justly, and says that in Christ there is "neither bond nor free" (Gal 3:28).

A secondary wife, often a servant, with fewer rights than a full wife; her children could inherit only if the father allowed. The Bible tells the stories plainly and shows the trouble that came from it, while God's purpose from the beginning was one husband and one wife (Gen 2:24; Matt 19:4-6).

Men who were castrated, often to serve in royal palaces and in charge of the king's women; the word came to mean any high court official. Isaiah promised faithful eunuchs a name in God's house, and the Ethiopian eunuch was one of the first Gentiles to believe.

A trusted officer who served the king's wine, tasting it first to guard against poison. Being close to the king, he had great influence, which is how Nehemiah could ask the king of Persia to let him rebuild Jerusalem.

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: The dead were buried quickly, usually the same day, wrapped in linen with spices, in a family tomb: often a cave or a room cut in rock, closed by a large stone. Families mourned loudly, often hiring flute players and wailing women, and mourning lasted seven days or more. This is the background to the burial of Jesus and the women coming with spices on the third day.

Taking off one's sandals showed reverence on holy ground. Handing over a sandal sealed the transfer of land or rights (Ruth 4:7). Untying a master's sandals was a slave's lowest task; John the Baptist said he was not worthy even to do that for Christ.

In a dry land wells were precious, dug deep and sometimes fought over. Women drew water at evening, so the well was a meeting place where Abraham's servant found Rebekah, Jacob met Rachel and Moses met Zipporah, and where Jesus met the Samaritan woman at noon. Cisterns were pits cut in rock to store rainwater; an empty one could be used as a prison, as for Joseph and Jeremiah.

A walled enclosure where flocks were kept safe at night, with one opening. Several shepherds might share one fold; each called his own sheep, who knew his voice. Some shepherds slept across the opening themselves, which helps explain Jesus' words "I am the door of the sheep" (John 10:7).

Houses had flat roofs, reached by outside stairs, used for drying crops, sleeping in hot weather, praying and talking. A wall around the edge was required so no one fell. The friends of the paralysed man dug through the roof of earth and branches to lower him to Jesus.

Grain was ground daily between two round stones, usually by women working a hand mill at home. A large millstone turned by a donkey was too heavy to lift, the picture Jesus used of what it would be better to drown with than to cause a little one to stumble. The Law forbade taking a millstone as a pledge, since a family's food depended on it.

Wine was kept in the whole skins of goats, sewn up. New wine still fermenting would stretch a skin; an old, dry skin would burst. Jesus used this to show that the new life he brings cannot be poured into old forms.

A pit cut in rock where grapes were trodden underfoot, with the juice running into a lower vat. Gideon threshed wheat in a winepress to hide from the Midianites. (In the prophets and Revelation it pictures God's judgment: see Symbols.)

A seal was an engraved stone or ring pressed into clay or wax to sign a document or show ownership; a king's seal carried his full authority. Pharaoh gave Joseph his signet ring; the tomb of Jesus was sealed so no one could open it.

Books were long strips of papyrus or leather, rolled on rods, read by unrolling from one side to the other. In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus was handed the scroll of Isaiah, found the place, read, rolled it up and sat down to teach.

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: Men who exchanged the many foreign coins pilgrims brought into the coins accepted for the temple tax, charging a fee. They set up their tables in the temple courts; Jesus overturned them, saying his Father's house should be a house of prayer.

column4: tribute|tribute money|half shekel|half a shekel|temple tax|two-drachma tax|two drachma|didrachma|drachma|tax|shekel
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: Every Jewish man paid half a shekel a year for the upkeep of the temple, first commanded as a ransom when the people were counted. Jesus paid it for himself and Peter with a coin found in a fish's mouth.

column4: corban|devoted to god|gift devoted to god|a gift|gift to god
column10: A Hebrew word for an offering given to God. Some declared their money "corban", dedicated to God, so they would not have to use it to support their parents; Jesus condemned this as cancelling God's command to honour father and mother.

The Roman way of putting slaves, rebels and criminals to death: nailed or tied to a wooden cross and left to die slowly in public, often after flogging. It was the most shameful death, and the Law said one hanged on a tree was under God's curse (Deut 21:23; Gal 3:13). Paul preached "Christ crucified" as God's power to save.

column4: centurion|centurions|centurion's|captain of a hundred|commander of a hundred
column10: An officer in the Roman army in charge of about a hundred soldiers. Several centurions in the New Testament are good men: one whose faith amazed Jesus, the one at the cross who said "truly this was the Son of God", and Cornelius, the first Gentile believer.

column4: praetorium|common hall|judgment hall|hall of judgment|governor's headquarters|governor's palace|palace guard|praetorian guard|imperial guard|headquarters
column10: The Praetorium was the Roman governor's residence and court. In Jerusalem Pilate judged Jesus there; the Jewish leaders would not go in, so as not to be made unclean before the Passover. In Rome the Praetorian Guard watched Paul in prison, and he wrote that the gospel had become known to them all.

Being a Roman citizen gave valuable rights: a citizen could not be flogged or punished without a trial, and could appeal to Caesar. Paul was born a citizen and used his rights to protect himself and the gospel; he reminded the Philippians that their true citizenship is in heaven.

The Roman emperor counted the people of his provinces in order to tax them. Because of Caesar Augustus' decree, Joseph and Mary travelled to Bethlehem, the town of David's family, where Jesus was born, as Micah had foretold.

column4: adoption|adopted|adoption as sons|adoption to sonship|sonship|adoption of children|adopted as his sons
column10: Under Roman law an adopted son received all the rights of a natural son, including the father's name and inheritance, and his old debts were cancelled. Paul uses it to describe believers: brought into God's family, able to call him "Abba, Father", and heirs with Christ.

column4: middle wall of partition|dividing wall|wall of hostility|partition|wall|barrier
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: In the temple a low stone wall kept Gentiles out of the inner courts, with notices warning of death for any who passed it. Paul was nearly killed when he was thought to have brought a Gentile in. He writes that Christ has broken down the "middle wall of partition" between Jew and Gentile.

column4: wise men|magi|magi from the east|wise men from the east
column10: Learned men from the east (perhaps Persia or Babylon) who studied the stars. They followed a star to Bethlehem and worshipped the child Jesus with gold, frankincense and myrrh: the first Gentiles to honour him as king. The Bible does not say how many there were.

column4: one|one lord|one god|one body|one spirit|one flesh
column10: Unity and the uniqueness of God: "the Lord our God is one Lord" (Deut 6:4). Jesus prayed that his people "may be one", and Paul writes of "one body, and one Spirit... one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all" (Eph 4:4-6).
Witness and confirmation: "at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established" (Deut 19:15). Jesus sent his disciples out two by two.

Completeness and the work of God; above all, the third day of Christ's resurrection: "he was buried, and... rose again the third day according to the scriptures" (1 Cor 15:4). The threefold "Holy, holy, holy" and the threefold name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit have long been read as pointing to the Trinity.

column4: four|fourth|four corners|four winds|four living creatures|four beasts
column10: The whole created world, with its four directions: the four winds, the four corners of the earth, the four living creatures around the throne and the four horsemen sent through the earth.

column4: six|six hundred threescore and six|666|six hundred sixty six|six hundred and sixty six|threescore|sixty
column10: Here is wisdom. Let him that hath understanding count the number of the beast: for it is the number of a man; and his number is Six hundred threescore and six (Rev 13:18). Because six falls short of seven, the number of completeness, the traditional reading is that it marks the beast as a human counterfeit that always falls short of God. Many have tried to name a person from it; the Bible does not say who it is. Nebuchadnezzar's idol was sixty cubits high and six wide.

column4: seven|seventh|sevenfold|seven times|sevens|seventy times seven|seven spirits|seven churches|seven seals|seven trumpets|seven vials|seven bowls|seven stars|seven lamps|seven eyes|seven horns
column10: Completeness and perfection, especially God's own work, from the seven days of creation and the seventh-day Sabbath. Sevens run through the Law (sprinkling seven times), the fall of Jericho, and above all Revelation: seven churches, seals, trumpets and bowls, and the Lamb's seven horns and eyes (perfect power and knowledge). Jesus' "seventy times seven" means forgiving without limit.

A new beginning, one beyond the complete seven: boys were circumcised on the eighth day, eight people came through the flood into a new world, and Jesus rose on the first day of a new week. This reading is traditional but less certain than for seven or twelve.

column4: ten|tenth|ten commandments|ten horns|ten days|ten virgins|ten talents|ten pieces of silver|ten servants|ten pounds
column10: A complete or full number, as of the fingers on two hands: the Ten Commandments, the ten plagues, ten virgins in the parable. In Daniel and Revelation ten horns are ten kings, the full sum of worldly power.

column4: twelve|twelfth|twelve tribes|twelve apostles|twelve stars|twelve gates|twelve foundations|twelve thrones|twelve disciples
column10: God's people, complete: the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles of the Lamb. The new Jerusalem has twelve gates with the tribes' names and twelve foundations with the apostles' names: Old and New Testament people of God together.

column4: thirty|thirty pieces of silver|thirty shekels|thirty silver coins
column10: The price of a slave under the Law (Exod 21:32). Zechariah was paid thirty pieces of silver as an insult and threw them to the potter; Judas betrayed Jesus for the same sum, and it was used to buy the potter's field.

column4: forty|fortieth|forty days|forty years|forty days and forty nights
column10: A time of testing, trial and preparation: forty days of rain in the flood, Moses forty days on Sinai, Israel forty years in the wilderness, Elijah forty days to Horeb, and Jesus forty days tempted in the wilderness. Jesus appeared to his disciples for forty days after he rose.
Freedom and fulfilment: the fiftieth year was the Jubilee, when liberty was proclaimed, and the fiftieth day after Passover was Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit was given.

column4: seventy|threescore and ten|seventy elders|seventy years|seventy two|seventy-two|other seventy
column10: A full number of people or years: seventy elders shared Moses' work, the exile in Babylon lasted seventy years as Jeremiah foretold, and Jesus sent out seventy (some manuscripts, seventy-two) to go ahead of him, often linked with the seventy nations of Genesis 10.

column4: seventy weeks|seventy sevens|weeks|sevens|threescore and two weeks|sixty-two weeks|one week
column10: Gabriel told Daniel that "seventy weeks" (seventy sevens, of years) were decreed "to make an end of sins... and to bring in everlasting righteousness" and to anoint the most Holy. Traditional Protestant interpreters count the weeks of years from the decree to rebuild Jerusalem to the coming and death of the Messiah, Christ, "cut off, but not for himself" (Dan 9:26).

column3: Three and a half (a time, times and half a time)
column4: time and times and the dividing of time|time and times and half a time|a time and times and half a time|forty and two months|forty-two months|42 months|thousand two hundred and threescore days|1 260 days|1260 days|three days and an half|three and a half days|months|days|time
column10: Half of seven: a broken, limited time of trouble that God has set and will cut short. It appears as "a time, and times, and half a time", 42 months and 1,260 days: the time the holy city is trampled, the woman is kept safe in the wilderness and the beast is allowed to act. However hard the time, it is limited, and it ends at God's appointed time.

column4: 144|hundred and forty and four thousand|hundred forty-four thousand|one hundred and forty-four thousand|144 000|one hundred forty-four thousand
column10: Twelve times twelve times a thousand: God's people complete, every one sealed and kept safe, none missing. Revelation 7 lists twelve thousand from each tribe, then John sees "a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations" (Rev 7:9). Many traditional interpreters see the two as the same people of God seen two ways.

column4: thousand years|thousand|a thousand years|1 000 years|1000 years
column10: A thousand stands for a great, complete number ("the cattle upon a thousand hills", Ps 50:10), and "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years" (2 Pet 3:8). In Revelation 20 Satan is bound for a thousand years while the saints reign with Christ; Augustine and the Reformers read this as Christ's reign now, from his resurrection to his return, with Satan restrained so the gospel goes to the nations.

Jesus, the sacrifice for sin. John the Baptist called him "the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (John 1:29), fulfilling the Passover lamb and Isaiah's servant led "as a lamb to the slaughter". In Revelation the slain Lamb stands on the throne, worshipped by all heaven, and conquers.

Strength, courage and royal power. Jacob called Judah a lion, and Christ is "the Lion of the tribe of Judah" (Rev 5:5); the Lord's voice roars like a lion (Amos 3:8). But the devil too "walketh about, as a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour" (1 Pet 5:8). In Daniel 7 a lion with wings stands for Babylon.

The Holy Spirit, who came down on Jesus at his baptism "like a dove". The dove also stands for gentleness and innocence ("harmless as doves", Matt 10:16), for peace (the dove with the olive leaf after the flood), and in the Song of Songs for the beloved.

Satan, the deceiver. The serpent tempted Eve in Eden; Revelation names "that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world" (Rev 12:9) and shows the great red dragon defeated and bound. God's promise that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head (Gen 3:15) is read as the first promise of Christ.

When Israel was dying from snake bites, God told Moses to set a bronze snake on a pole: whoever looked at it lived. Jesus said, "as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up" on the cross, so that whoever believes may have eternal life.

Worldly kingdoms and powers that set themselves against God and his people. Daniel is told that his four beasts "are four kings, which shall arise out of the earth" (Dan 7:17). In Revelation the beast from the sea makes war on the saints and demands worship, but is thrown into the lake of fire.

Heavenly beings around God's throne, full of eyes, with the faces of a lion, an ox, a man and an eagle, crying "Holy, holy, holy". They show God's majesty and the worship of all creation. Since early times Christians have also linked the four faces with the four Gospels.

Power and strength, like the horns of a strong animal; "the horn of salvation" is the strong Saviour God raised up (Luke 1:69). In Daniel and Revelation horns are kings: "the ten horns out of this kingdom are ten kings" (Dan 7:24). The Lamb's seven horns show his perfect power.
God's care and strength: he carried Israel "on eagles' wings" out of Egypt, and those who wait on him "shall mount up with wings as eagles" (Isa 40:31). In Ezekiel 17 the eagles are great kings.

God's people: needing a shepherd, prone to wander, cared for and led. "All we like sheep have gone astray" (Isa 53:6); "we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture" (Ps 100:3). At the judgment Christ separates the sheep (the righteous) from the goats.

One who leads, feeds and protects God's people. "The Lord is my shepherd" (Ps 23:1). Kings and leaders were called shepherds, and the prophets condemned the bad ones. Jesus is "the good shepherd" who gives his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and church leaders are shepherds under him.

False teachers and the enemies of God's people, who come to tear the flock: "false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves" (Matt 7:15). In Isaiah the wolf living with the lamb pictures the peace of God's coming kingdom.
Jesus called fishermen to become "fishers of men" (Matt 4:19), gathering people into God's kingdom. In the parable of the net, the catch of good and bad fish pictures the final judgment.

Swarms of locusts that strip the land bare stand for God's judgment and invading armies; Joel describes an army like locusts. God promises, "I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten" (Joel 2:25).

In Zechariah horses of different colours are God's messengers patrolling the earth. In Revelation 6 four riders bring conquest (white), war (red), famine (black) and death (pale). In Revelation 19 Christ himself rides a white horse, "Faithful and True", to judge and make war in righteousness.

God's people. Israel was the vine God planted and cared for, which should have borne good fruit: "the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel" (Isa 5:7). Jesus said, "I am the true vine, ye are the branches" (John 15:5): life and fruit come only from staying joined to him.

A title of the Messiah: a new shoot growing from the cut-down stump of Jesse, David's father. "I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign" (Jer 23:5). The New Testament sees it fulfilled in Jesus, "the root and the offspring of David" (Rev 22:16).

Israel, expected to bear fruit for God. Jesus cursed a fig tree full of leaves but with no fruit, a picture of religion with no true faith, and told the parable of the barren fig tree given one more year. "Every man under his fig tree" pictures peace and plenty (Mic 4:4).

God's people, rich and fruitful: "I am like a green olive tree in the house of God" (Ps 52:8). Paul pictures Israel as a cultivated olive tree into which Gentile believers, wild branches, have been grafted. In Zechariah and Revelation two olive trees supply oil: God's anointed witnesses.
The tall, strong cedars of Lebanon stand for greatness and lasting strength: "the righteous shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon" (Ps 92:12). Proud nations are pictured as cedars God brings down.
The tiniest of seeds that grows into a great plant: God's kingdom, small in its beginning, grows to fill the world. Faith as small as a mustard seed, trusting a great God, can move mountains.

In the parable of the sower, "the seed is the word of God" (Luke 8:11), received differently by different hearts. A grain of wheat dying to bear much fruit pictures Jesus' death and our resurrection. The promised "seed" of the woman and of Abraham is Christ (Gal 3:16).

The righteous and the wicked, growing together until the harvest, when they are separated. Chaff, light and worthless, blows away: "the ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away" (Ps 1:4).

The curse of sin on the ground (Gen 3:18) and the worries and riches that choke God's word (Matt 13:22). Jesus wore a crown of thorns, bearing the curse; Paul's "thorn in the flesh" was a painful trial that taught him God's grace is enough.
How short human life is: "All flesh is grass... The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever" (Isa 40:6-8).

The tree in Eden whose fruit gave everlasting life, closed to Adam and Eve after the fall. It appears again in the new Jerusalem, open to all who are washed and made clean, "for the healing of the nations" (Rev 22:2): eternal life restored.

The person who delights in God's word and trusts in him is "like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season" (Ps 1:3): steady, fruitful and green even in drought.

A small bushy plant used to sprinkle blood or water in cleansing rites, as on the doorposts at Passover. David prayed, "Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean" (Ps 51:7). Jesus was offered sour wine on a hyssop branch at the cross.

Authority and rule. "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah" (Gen 49:10) promises a lasting king; the Messiah rules the nations "with a rod of iron" (Ps 2:9). Aaron's rod that budded showed God's chosen priest. The shepherd's rod and staff in Psalm 23 mean protection and guidance.

What gives and sustains life. "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God" (Matt 4:4). Jesus said, "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35); at the Last Supper the broken bread stood for his body given for us.

column4: manna|bread from heaven|bread of heaven|hidden manna
column10: The bread God sent from heaven each morning to feed Israel in the wilderness for forty years. Jesus said he is the true bread from heaven: "your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead... if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever" (John 6:49-51).

A person's portion or lot from God: a cup of blessing and salvation, or the cup of God's wrath against sin. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed that "this cup" might pass from him, yet drank it for us. At the Last Supper the cup of wine is "the new testament in my blood".

Joy and blessing: the coming kingdom is a feast "of wines on the lees" (Isa 25:6), and Jesus' first sign turned water into the best wine. New wine pictures the new life he brings. In Revelation Babylon makes the nations drunk with the wine of her immorality, and the wicked drink the wine of God's wrath.

Life, cleansing and the Holy Spirit. God is "the fountain of living waters" (Jer 2:13); Jesus offers living water that becomes "a well of water springing up into everlasting life" (John 4:14), which John explains is the Spirit (John 7:39). The river of life flows from God's throne in the new creation.

God's presence, truth, holiness and life. "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all" (1 John 1:5). Jesus is "the light of the world" (John 8:12), and his people are to shine as lights. God's word is "a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path".
Sin, ignorance and evil, and the realm of Satan from which God rescues his people: "who hath delivered us from the power of darkness" (Col 1:13). "Outer darkness" is the final separation from God.

God's word giving guidance ("a lamp unto my feet", Ps 119:105), the life of the righteous, and the witness of believers, not to be hidden under a basket. The wise virgins' lamps with oil picture being ready for Christ's coming.

In Revelation the Bible explains it: "the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches" (Rev 1:20). The church holds out the light of Christ, who walks among the lampstands; a church that loses its first love may have its lampstand removed.

Salt preserves and flavours. Jesus called his disciples "the salt of the earth" (Matt 5:13), a good influence in a decaying world. A "covenant of salt" is a lasting, unbreakable covenant; Christians' speech should be "seasoned with salt" (Col 4:6).

A little leaven spreads through the whole lump of dough. Most often it pictures sin and false teaching that spread: "beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy" (Luke 12:1). In one parable it shows the hidden growth of God's kingdom (Matt 13:33).

The Holy Spirit and God's blessing and joy. Kings and priests were anointed with oil when God's Spirit came on them for their work; Christ was anointed "with the oil of gladness" (Heb 1:9). Believers too have "an unction from the Holy One" (1 John 2:20).

Life given in death. "The life of the flesh is in the blood... it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul" (Lev 17:11). The blood of the Passover lamb saved Israel; the blood of Christ, shed on the cross, cleanses from all sin and seals the new covenant.
God's holy presence ("our God is a consuming fire", Heb 12:29), his purifying work, like a refiner's fire, and his judgment on sin. The Holy Spirit came at Pentecost as tongues of fire.

God's glorious presence, both shown and hidden. A pillar of cloud led Israel and filled the tabernacle and temple; a cloud covered Jesus at the transfiguration and received him at his ascension. The Son of Man comes "with the clouds of heaven" (Dan 7:13; Rev 1:7).

The Holy Spirit: in Hebrew and Greek the same word means wind, breath and spirit. God breathed life into Adam; the wind of the Spirit gave life to the dry bones in Ezekiel; Jesus compared new birth by the Spirit to the wind (John 3:8) and breathed on his disciples, saying "Receive ye the Holy Ghost".

God himself, firm, safe and unchanging: "The Lord is my rock, and my fortress" (Ps 18:2). The rock that gave water in the wilderness "was Christ" (1 Cor 10:4). A life built on Jesus' words is a house built on rock.

column4: cornerstone|corner stone|chief corner stone|head of the corner|capstone|chief cornerstone|stone|cornerstone of the foundation
column10: Christ: "the stone which the builders rejected is become the head of the corner" (Ps 118:22), rejected by his own people but made the foundation of God's new temple, the church. Believers are "lively stones" built on him (1 Pet 2:5).

column4: stone|mountain|cut out without hands|cut without hands
column10: In Nebuchadnezzar's dream a stone cut out without human hands smashes the great statue and grows into a mountain filling the earth. Daniel explains it: "the God of heaven shall set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed" (Dan 2:44): the kingdom of God, which traditional interpreters see coming in Christ.

Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of a statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay. Daniel explains that the gold head is Babylon, followed by lesser kingdoms; traditional interpreters name them Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome, all to be swept away by God's everlasting kingdom.

The way in to God and his salvation. "I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved" (John 10:9). The narrow gate leads to life. Christ "stands at the door and knocks", and an "open door" means an opportunity for the gospel.

The way of life one follows: the way of the righteous or of the wicked (Ps 1:6). Jesus said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (John 14:6), and the first Christians were called followers of "the Way".

Authority to open and shut, to allow in or keep out. Christ holds "the keys of hell and of death" (Rev 1:18) and "the key of David" (Rev 3:7); he gave Peter "the keys of the kingdom of heaven", authority to open the kingdom through preaching the gospel.

The word of God, sharp and powerful: "the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God" (Eph 6:17); "sharper than any twoedged sword" (Heb 4:12). From Christ's mouth comes a sharp sword, his word of judgment. Jesus' "sword" in Matt 10:34 is the division the gospel brings.

Paul's picture of how believers stand against evil: the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, feet ready with the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, God's word, all with prayer (Eph 6:11-18).

column4: crown|crowns|crowned|crown of life|crown of glory|crown of righteousness|crown of thorns
column10: Royal rule and honour, and the reward God gives the faithful: "a crown of life" (Jas 1:12; Rev 2:10), "a crown of righteousness" (2 Tim 4:8). Jesus wore a crown of thorns before he was crowned with glory; the elders in heaven cast their crowns before God's throne.

God's rule over all. Isaiah saw "the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up" (Isa 6:1); Revelation centres on the throne in heaven, where the Lamb shares the throne. Believers may come boldly to "the throne of grace" (Heb 4:16).

column4: white robes|white robe|robes|robe|white raiment|raiment|garments|garment|fine linen|linen|clothed in white|white
column10: Purity and righteousness given by God. The redeemed "have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb" (Rev 7:14); "the fine linen is the righteousness of saints" (Rev 19:8). In Zechariah God takes away the high priest's filthy clothes and gives him clean ones.

A seal marks ownership and keeps something secure. Believers are "sealed with that holy Spirit of promise" (Eph 1:13), marked as God's own. In Revelation only the Lamb is worthy to open the scroll with seven seals, the unfolding of God's purposes in history.

column4: book of life|lamb's book of life|book|books|written in heaven
column10: God's record of those who belong to him and will have eternal life. Jesus told his disciples to rejoice that "your names are written in heaven" (Luke 10:20); only "they which are written in the Lamb's book of life" enter the new Jerusalem.

God's call and announcement: to gather, to warn, to battle and to worship. "The trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised" (1 Cor 15:52) at Christ's return. In Revelation seven trumpets announce God's judgments, the last proclaiming that the kingdoms of the world have become Christ's.
In Revelation, golden bowls full of incense are "the prayers of saints" (Rev 5:8). Seven bowls full of God's wrath are poured out on the earth in the final judgments.
Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense (Ps 141:2). In Revelation the incense rising before God's throne is the prayers of his people, heard and answered.

column3: The temple: God's people and Christ's body
column10: Jesus spoke of "the temple of his body" (John 2:21), raised in three days. Since God now dwells by his Spirit in his people, the church and each believer are God's temple. In the new Jerusalem there is no temple, "for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it".

The tabernacle where God dwelt with Israel points to Christ: "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt (literally, pitched his tent) among us" (John 1:14), and to the end, when "the tabernacle of God is with men" (Rev 21:3). Paul and Peter call the body an earthly tent we shall one day put off.

The wooden bar on the necks of working animals: a picture of servitude and burdens, like slavery in Egypt or rule by a foreign king. Jesus offers his own yoke, "easy" and "light" (Matt 11:30), and Paul warns not to return to "the yoke of bondage" of keeping the Law to be saved.

God's covenant love for his people is pictured as a marriage: "thy Maker is thine husband" (Isa 54:5). Christ is the Bridegroom and the church his bride, whom he loved and gave himself for; history ends with "the marriage supper of the Lamb" (Rev 19:9).

Turning from God to idols is pictured as a wife's unfaithfulness. The prophets used this to show the depth of Israel's betrayal and of God's grief and love; Hosea was told to marry an unfaithful wife as a living picture. Jesus spoke of "an evil and adulterous generation". In Revelation the great harlot is Babylon, the world's seductive power against God.

column4: babylon|babylon the great|great city|the great city
column10: In Revelation, Babylon is "that great city, which reigneth over the kings of the earth" (Rev 17:18): the world's power, wealth and pride set against God, traditionally seen first in pagan Rome. Its sudden fall is certain. Peter seems to call Rome "Babylon" too (1 Pet 5:13).

column4: new jerusalem|jerusalem|zion|sion|mount zion|mount sion|holy city|heavenly jerusalem|city of god
column10: Jerusalem's hill Zion, where God's temple stood, came to stand for God's dwelling with his people, and finally for the heavenly city: "ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem" (Heb 12:22). The new Jerusalem comes down from heaven at the end, as a bride.

column4: mountain|mountains|mount|hill|holy mountain|holy hill|mountain of the lord
column10: God's dwelling and rule. "In the last days... the mountain of the Lord's house shall be established in the top of the mountains, and all nations shall flow unto it" (Isa 2:2): God's kingdom drawing the nations. Faith can "move mountains", the greatest obstacles.

The restless, threatening sea stands for chaos, evil and the troubled nations: "the wicked are like the troubled sea" (Isa 57:20); the beasts rise out of it. Revelation explains, "the waters which thou sawest... are peoples, and multitudes, and nations" (Rev 17:15); in the new creation "there was no more sea".
The sign of God's covenant never again to destroy the earth by flood. A rainbow surrounds God's throne in Ezekiel and Revelation: his glory joined with faithful mercy.

column4: star|stars|morning star|day star|daystar|bright and morning star|star out of jacob
column10: Countless descendants (Abraham's offspring "as the stars of the heaven"), rulers and heavenly beings. "The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches" (Rev 1:20). Balaam foresaw "a Star out of Jacob", fulfilled in Christ, "the bright and morning star" (Rev 22:16). The wise "shall shine... as the stars for ever".

God's glory, faithfulness and the coming Messiah: "unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings" (Mal 4:2). The sun darkened and moon turned to blood are signs of the day of the Lord. In the new Jerusalem there is no need of sun or moon, for God is its light.

Gathering people: into God's kingdom through the gospel ("the harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few", Matt 9:37), and at the end of the age in judgment ("the harvest is the end of the world", Matt 13:39). "Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" (Gal 6:7).

As grapes are trodden in the winepress, God's judgment crushes his enemies: "I have trodden the winepress alone" (Isa 63:3). In Revelation the harvest of the earth is thrown into "the great winepress of the wrath of God", which Christ treads.

John the Baptist said of Christ: "whose fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire" (Matt 3:12): his coming separates the true from the false.

God is the potter and we are the clay: "we are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand" (Isa 64:8). He has the right to shape people and nations. Paul says we hold the treasure of the gospel "in earthen vessels", so the power is seen to be God's.

As metal is melted to burn away impurities, God uses trials to purify his people: "he is like a refiner's fire" (Mal 3:2). Faith tested this way is "much more precious than of gold that perisheth" (1 Pet 1:7).

Being cleansed from sin. "Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow" (Isa 1:18); "wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow" (Ps 51:7). The redeemed have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb.

The outward sign of the covenant pointed to an inward change: "circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart" (Deut 10:16). Paul says true circumcision is "that of the heart, in the spirit" (Rom 2:29), God's work cutting away the old sinful nature.

column4: heart|hearts|stony heart|heart of stone|heart of flesh|new heart|tables of stone|fleshy tables
column10: A new heart also will I give you... I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh (Ezek 36:26): God's promise to change his people from within, writing his law on their hearts in the new covenant.

column4: right hand|right hand of god|right hand of power|right hand of the majesty
column10: The place of honour, power and authority. After rising, Christ "sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high" (Heb 1:3), ruling and praying for his people, as Psalm 110 foretold: "Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool".

column4: arm|arms|stretched out arm|outstretched arm|mighty arm|holy arm|arm of the lord
column10: God's power in action, especially to save: he brought Israel out of Egypt "with a stretched out arm". Isaiah asks, "to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?" (Isa 53:1), and John sees it answered in Jesus.

column4: footstool|foot stool|under his feet|under thy feet
column10: Complete rule and victory: the earth is God's footstool (Isa 66:1), and Christ reigns until all his enemies are made his footstool (Ps 110:1; Heb 10:13).

column4: dust|ashes|dust of the earth|dust of the ground
column10: Human weakness and mortality: "dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" (Gen 3:19). God "remembereth that we are dust" (Ps 103:14). Abraham's descendants would be as many as the dust of the earth.
For believers death is called sleep, because it is not the end: they will wake at the resurrection. "Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep" (John 11:11).

column4: born again|born|birth|regeneration|begotten|born anew|born of god|born of the spirit
column10: Jesus told Nicodemus, "Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God" (John 3:3): a new beginning of life from God by his Spirit, as real as natural birth.

The ark saved Noah's family through the judgment of the flood. Peter links it with baptism, and traditional Christian teaching sees the ark as a picture of salvation in Christ, the one place of safety when judgment comes.

column4: sign|sign of jonas|sign of jonah|jonas|jonah|three days
column10: Jonah's three days in the great fish pointed to Jesus: "as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matt 12:40), before rising again.

The king of Salem and priest of the Most High God who blessed Abraham. With no recorded beginning or end, he pictures Christ, "a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec" (Ps 110:4), both King and Priest, whose priesthood never ends.
Adam was "the figure of him that was to come" (Rom 5:14). As all die through the first Adam's sin, so all who are in Christ, "the last Adam", are made alive; he is the head of a new humanity.

column4: son of man|one like the son of man|one like unto the son of man|one like a son of man
column10: In Daniel's vision "one like the Son of man" comes with the clouds of heaven and receives an everlasting kingdom. Jesus took this as his favourite title for himself, and at his trial claimed Daniel's vision as his own.
God himself, eternal, seated on his fiery throne in judgment, his clothing white as snow and his hair like pure wool: the everlasting King who gives the kingdom to the Son of Man.

column4: milk and honey|flowing with milk and honey|floweth with milk and honey|milk|honey
column10: A land flowing with milk and honey: the rich plenty of the land God promised, good for flocks (milk) and full of flowers and fruit (honey).

Milk is the simple first teaching for young believers; solid food is deeper teaching for those grown mature. New believers should long for "the sincere milk of the word" to grow (1 Pet 2:2), but not stay babies.

A place of testing, humbling and dependence on God, where Israel learned that man lives by every word of God, and where Jesus was tempted forty days. It is also where God meets and protects his people, and where the way of the Lord is prepared.

column4: rest|sabbath rest|sabbath-rest|my rest|his rest|enter into rest
column10: The promised land was Israel's rest, but Hebrews says a greater rest remains for God's people: ceasing from our own works and trusting Christ, and the eternal rest to come. "Come unto me... and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28).

The visible results of a life, good or bad: "by their fruits ye shall know them" (Matt 7:20). "The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance" (Gal 5:22-23), growing in those joined to Christ.

The kingdom of heaven, worth more than everything else: a man sells all he has to buy a field with hidden treasure, a merchant to buy one pearl of great price. Jesus told us to lay up treasure in heaven.
The church: "now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular" (1 Cor 12:27). Like the parts of a body, believers are joined to one another and to Christ the head, each with a part to play.
Christ is "the head of the body, the church" (Col 1:18): its source of life, its ruler and the one it grows up into.

God's people are a building he is making, "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone" (Eph 2:20). "Other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ" (1 Cor 3:11).
The Christian life is a race to be run with endurance, looking to Jesus, the goal and the prize. Paul at the end could say, "I have finished my course, I have kept the faith" (2 Tim 4:7).

The prophet as a lookout on the city wall, warning of danger: "I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel" (Ezek 3:17). If he fails to warn, he is responsible; church leaders too "watch for your souls" (Heb 13:17).

column4: wings|wing|under his wings|shadow of thy wings
column10: God's tender protection, like a bird sheltering its young: "he shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust" (Ps 91:4). Jesus longed to gather Jerusalem "as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings".
God's protection of his people: "The name of the Lord is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe" (Prov 18:10); "God is our refuge and strength" (Ps 46:1).
Christian hope in God's promise is "an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast" (Heb 6:19), holding firm in storms because it is fixed in Christ, who has gone ahead into God's presence.
Ancient mirrors of polished metal gave only a dim image: "now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). James likens God's word to a mirror that shows us as we are.

column3: The mark and the name on the forehead
column4: mark|forehead|foreheads|seal of god|his name|the mark of the beast
column10: Showing who a person belongs to. God's servants are sealed with his name on their foreheads; those who follow the beast take its mark. Traditional interpreters read it as the outward sign of a person's loyalty, whether to God or to the world's power.
The abyss: the prison of evil spirits, from which the demons begged Jesus not to send them, and where Satan is bound in Revelation 20.

column4: four winds|four corners|corners of the earth|four quarters|winds
column10: North, south, east and west: the whole earth. The elect are gathered "from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other" (Matt 24:31).

Two prophets in Revelation 11 who testify for God, are killed by the beast, and are raised and taken up to heaven. They are described like Moses and Elijah; many traditional interpreters see in them the faithful witness of God's people, which cannot finally be silenced.

column3: The woman clothed with the sun
column4: woman|a woman clothed with the sun
column10: A woman crowned with twelve stars gives birth to the male child who will rule the nations, Christ, while the dragon tries to destroy him. Traditional Protestant interpreters see her as God's people, Israel and the church, from whom the Messiah came and whom God protects.
Purity, holiness and victory: the shining white of the transfigured Christ, the white robes of the redeemed, the white horse of the conqueror and the great white throne of judgment.

The colour of blood: sin ("though your sins be as scarlet", Isa 1:18), war (the red horse of Rev 6), and the dragon and the harlot. Rahab's scarlet cord, which saved her house, has often been seen as a picture of salvation through blood.
Purple dye was rare and costly, so purple meant royalty and wealth. The soldiers put a purple robe on Jesus to mock him as king; the rich man of the parable "was clothed in purple and fine linen".
In Revelation's four horses, black stands for famine and the pale (greenish-grey, the colour of a corpse) horse for death. "Blackness of darkness" is the doom of false teachers (Jude 13).

The beauty, worth and glory of God and of the new Jerusalem, whose walls and foundations are of precious stones, its gates of pearl and its street of pure gold. The twelve stones echo those on the high priest's breastpiece, bearing the names of God's people.

column4: tabernacle|tent of meeting|tabernacle of the congregation|tabernacle of witness|tabernacle of the testimony|tent of the testimony|tabernacle of the lord|tent of the lord
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: The holy tent Israel made in the wilderness at God's command, where he dwelt among his people. It could be taken down and carried; it stood in a courtyard with the altar and basin, and inside were the Holy Place (with the lampstand, the table of bread and the incense altar) and the Most Holy Place (with the ark). Hebrews calls it a copy and shadow of the true sanctuary in heaven, where Christ ministers.

column4: temple|temples|house of the lord|house of god|temple courts|temple of the lord
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: God's house in Jerusalem, where the sacrifices were offered. Solomon built the first temple (about 960 BC); Babylon destroyed it in 586 BC. The second temple was built after the exile and greatly enlarged by Herod the Great; this is the temple Jesus knew, with its large courts where people bought animals and changed money. The Romans destroyed it in AD 70, as Jesus had foretold.

column4: most holy place|holy of holies|holiest of all|the holiest|inner sanctuary|most holy room|the oracle|most holy
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: The innermost room of the tabernacle and temple, a perfect cube, where the ark of the covenant stood and God's presence dwelt. A thick curtain shut it off; only the high priest could go in, once a year on the Day of Atonement, with blood. Hebrews says Christ's death opened the way into God's presence for all who trust him (Heb 10:19-20).

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: The heavy woven curtain between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place, embroidered with cherubim. When Jesus died it was torn in two from top to bottom, showing that the way to God was opened. Hebrews calls Christ's body the veil through which we may now come near (Heb 10:20).

column4: ark of the covenant|ark of the testimony|ark of god|ark of the lord|ark of your might|ark of thy strength|ark of the covenant of the lord|ark of the covenant of god|ark of the law|the ark
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: A wooden chest overlaid with gold, holding the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, with Aaron's rod and a jar of manna. Its lid, the mercy seat, had two golden cherubim; God said he would meet with Israel there. It went before Israel through the Jordan and around Jericho, and stood in the Most Holy Place; it was lost when Babylon took Jerusalem.

column4: mercy seat|mercyseat|atonement cover|cover of atonement|place of atonement|atonement lid
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: The gold lid of the ark of the covenant, between the cherubim, where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement to cover the people's sins. Paul uses the same Greek word for Christ, whom God "set forth to be a propitiation" (Rom 3:25): the place where sin is covered and God's mercy met.

column4: altar|altars|altar of burnt offering|bronze altar|brasen altar|altar of the lord
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: A raised place of earth, stone or bronze where sacrifices were offered to God. Abraham and the patriarchs built altars where God met them; at the tabernacle and temple, the great bronze altar stood in the courtyard and its fire was never to go out. Altars to Baal and other gods were to be torn down.

column4: horns of the altar|horns of the altars|horn of the altar
column10: Projections like horns at the four corners of the altar. Blood of the sin offering was put on them. A person who fled to the altar and took hold of its horns was asking for God's protection from punishment (1 Kgs 1:50).

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: Sweet-smelling spices burned on the golden altar before the veil, morning and evening, by a priest chosen by lot. Its rising smoke pictured prayer going up to God (Ps 141:2; Rev 8:4). Zechariah was burning incense when the angel told him John the Baptist would be born.

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: The golden lampstand in the Holy Place, with a central shaft and six branches, its seven lamps kept burning with pure olive oil. It was the only light in the Holy Place. (In Zechariah and Revelation lampstands are symbols: see Symbols.)

column4: shewbread|showbread|bread of the presence|consecrated bread|holy bread|bread of presence|the bread of the presence|table of shewbread|sacred bread
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, set out every Sabbath on a gold table in the Holy Place, "before the face" of the Lord. Only priests could eat the old loaves. When David and his men were hungry the priest gave them this bread, and Jesus used it to show that mercy matters more than ritual.

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: An offering to God, most often an animal killed and offered on the altar, or grain, wine or oil. The Law set out several kinds: burnt, grain, peace, sin and guilt offerings. The blood of sacrifices made atonement for sin (Lev 17:11), pointing ahead to Christ, who "offered one sacrifice for sins for ever" (Heb 10:12). Christians are to offer themselves, praise and good deeds as living sacrifices.

column4: burnt offering|burnt offerings|burnt sacrifice|burnt sacrifices|whole burnt offering|whole burnt offerings
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: An animal wholly burned on the altar, nothing kept back: a picture of complete devotion to God. A lamb was offered every morning and every evening for the nation (the "continual" burnt offering).

column4: meat offering|meat offerings|grain offering|grain offerings|meal offering|meal offerings|cereal offering|cereal offerings|minchah
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: An offering of fine flour, with oil and frankincense but no yeast or honey, often baked into cakes. A handful was burned on the altar and the rest went to the priests. (The King James "meat offering" means food offering: "meat" then meant food.)

column4: peace offering|peace offerings|fellowship offering|fellowship offerings|sacrifice of peace offerings|sacrifices of peace offerings|offering of well-being|offerings of well-being
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: An offering of thanks or a vow, shared: the fat was burned to God, the priests had their portion, and the worshipper and family ate the rest in a joyful meal before the Lord. It pictured peace and fellowship with God.

column4: sin offering|sin offerings|offering for sin|purification offering|purification offerings
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: An offering for sins done without meaning to, or for uncleanness. Its blood was put on the altar's horns or sprinkled before the veil; for the priest or the nation the body was burned outside the camp. Hebrews notes that Jesus too "suffered outside the gate" (Heb 13:12).

column4: trespass offering|trespass offerings|guilt offering|guilt offerings|offering for guilt|compensation offering|reparation offering
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: An offering for wrongs that could be paid back, such as taking what belonged to God or to a neighbour. The wrongdoer repaid in full, plus a fifth, and offered a ram. Isaiah says the Servant of the Lord would make his life an offering for guilt (Isa 53:10).

column4: drink offering|drink offerings|libation|libations|poured out as a drink offering
column10: Wine poured out at the altar alongside other offerings. Paul twice speaks of his own life being "poured out" like a drink offering, in his ministry and at his coming death (Phil 2:17; 2 Tim 4:6).

column4: wave offering|wave offerings|heave offering|heave offerings|waved|wave them|wave it
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: Parts of an offering that were lifted up or waved before the Lord, showing they were given to him, and then given back to the priests as their share. The first sheaf of the harvest and the two loaves of Pentecost were waved in the same way.

column4: freewill offering|freewill offerings|free will offering|free will offerings|voluntary offering|voluntary offerings|willing offering
column10: An offering given gladly, not because the Law required it. The tabernacle was built from such gifts, and so much was given that Moses had to tell the people to stop (Exod 36:6).

column4: red heifer|ashes of an heifer|ashes of a heifer|ashes of the heifer|water of separation|water of purification|water of cleansing
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: A red cow without blemish was burned outside the camp, and its ashes mixed with water were sprinkled on anyone made unclean by touching a dead body. Hebrews contrasts this outward cleansing with the blood of Christ, which cleanses the conscience (Heb 9:13-14).

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: On the Day of Atonement two goats were chosen by lot. One was sacrificed; over the other the high priest confessed all Israel's sins, laying his hands on its head, and it was sent away into the wilderness, carrying their sins far off. It pictures sin removed "as far as the east is from the west" (Ps 103:12).

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: Aaron and his descendants, of the tribe of Levi, set apart to serve at the altar, offer sacrifices, burn incense, bless the people and teach God's law. In Jesus' day there were so many priests that they served in 24 divisions, a week at a time (Luke 1:8). The New Testament calls Christ the great High Priest and all believers a "royal priesthood" (1 Pet 2:9). Other nations had priests of their own gods too.

column4: high priest|high priests|chief priest|chief priests|leading priests|chief of the priests|high priest's
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: The head of the priests, at first from Aaron's line, who alone entered the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement and wore the ephod and breastpiece with the names of the twelve tribes. In Jesus' day the Romans appointed him; Annas and his son-in-law Caiaphas led the trial of Jesus. "Chief priests" were the leading priestly families on the council. Hebrews presents Jesus as the perfect High Priest who offered himself.

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: Members of the tribe of Levi, set apart to serve God in place of the firstborn of Israel. They carried the tabernacle, and later served in the temple as gatekeepers, singers, musicians and helpers of the priests; some taught the Law. They received no land of their own but lived on the tithes, in 48 towns spread through the tribes.

A priestly garment like a vest or apron.
