The high priest's ephod was of gold, blue, purple and scarlet, with two onyx stones on the shoulders engraved with the names of the tribes, and the breastpiece fastened to it. A simple linen ephod was worn by others serving God, like the boy Samuel and David dancing before the ark. Sometimes it was used to ask God's will, and Gideon's gold ephod became an idol.

column4: breastplate|breastpiece|breastplate of judgment|breastplate of judgement|breastpiece of judgment|breastpiece of decision|sacred chestpiece|chestpiece
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, The Temple: Its Ministry and Services
column10: A square pouch of fine woven cloth worn over the high priest's heart, set with twelve precious stones, each engraved with the name of a tribe: he carried the people before God. The Urim and Thummim were kept in it.

Two objects kept in the high priest's breastpiece, used to ask God for guidance in important matters. Their names mean "lights and perfections"; what they looked like and how they worked is not known. They are not mentioned as used after David's time.

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: In the Law, being "unclean" meant being unfit to come to God's sanctuary for a time, through things like touching a dead body, a skin disease, bodily discharges or eating forbidden animals. It was not always sin, but it taught that God is holy and his people must be set apart. Washing, waiting and offerings made a person clean again. Jesus taught that what truly defiles comes from the heart, and declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19).

Israel was to eat only "clean" animals: land animals that chew the cud and have split hooves, fish with fins and scales, and birds not on the forbidden list; no blood was to be eaten. These rules set Israel apart from the nations. In the New Testament God showed Peter that the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile was gone, and Paul taught that no food is unclean in itself.

column4: leprosy|leper|lepers|leprous|skin disease|skin diseases|infectious skin disease|defiling skin disease|serious skin disease|contagious skin disease|dreaded skin disease
column10: The Bible's "leprosy" covers several skin diseases (and even mould in cloth or walls). Someone with it was unclean: they lived outside the camp or town, tore their clothes and called out "Unclean!" so others kept away. Jesus touched lepers and healed them, and sent them to the priest to be declared clean.

The cutting away of the foreskin of every Jewish boy on the eighth day, the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and his descendants. "The uncircumcised" meant the Gentiles. The early church decided that Gentile believers did not need to be circumcised; Paul taught that what matters is the "circumcision of the heart" (Rom 2:29).

column4: purification|purifying|purified|days of her purification|days of purification
column10: After giving birth a mother was unclean for 40 days for a son and 80 for a daughter; then she brought a lamb and a pigeon or dove for a burnt offering and a sin offering. Mary offered "a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons", the offering allowed for the poor (Luke 2:24).

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: The priests washed their hands and feet before serving at the altar. By Jesus' day the Pharisees had added many washings of hands, cups and pots before eating, following "the tradition of the elders". Jesus rebuked them for keeping these while neglecting God's commandments (Mark 7:8).

Because God spared Israel's firstborn in Egypt, every firstborn son and male animal belonged to him. Firstborn animals were sacrificed; firstborn sons were "redeemed", bought back, for five shekels paid to the priests. Mary and Joseph brought the baby Jesus to the temple to present him to the Lord (Luke 2:22-23).

A tenth of crops and flocks, given to God. Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek. The Law gave the tithe to the Levites (who in turn gave a tenth of it to the priests); another tithe was eaten in celebration at the sanctuary, and every third year it was shared with the poor. Jesus said the Pharisees tithed even herbs but neglected justice, mercy and faith.

A solemn promise to God, often to give something or to do something if he answered a prayer, as Hannah vowed her son to the Lord. Vows were voluntary, but once made had to be kept; the Law gave rules for buying back things vowed. Paul once took a vow and cut his hair at its end.

column4: nazarite|nazarites|nazirite|nazirites|vow of a nazarite|vow of a nazirite|vow of separation|consecrated
column10: A man or woman who made a special vow to be set apart to God, for a time or for life. A Nazirite drank no wine and ate nothing from the vine, did not cut their hair, and did not go near a dead body. At the end the hair was shaved and burned with an offering. Samson, Samuel and probably John the Baptist were Nazirites from birth.

column4: laying on of hands|laying on of the hands|laid hands|laid his hands|laid their hands|lay hands|lay his hands|lay their hands|layeth his hands|put his hands|placed his hands|placed their hands
column10: Putting hands on a person or animal to bless, to heal, to set someone apart for a task, or (for a sacrifice) to show it stood in the worshipper's place. Jacob blessed Joseph's sons so; Moses laid hands on Joshua; the apostles laid hands on those sent out to serve.

Pouring oil on someone or something to set it apart for God. Priests, kings and some prophets were anointed; "Messiah" (Hebrew) and "Christ" (Greek) both mean "the Anointed One". Oil was also put on guests' heads as an honour, used on the sick, and on the bodies of the dead.

column4: synagogue|synagogues|ruler of the synagogue|synagogue ruler|synagogue leader|rulers of the synagogue|leader of the synagogue
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: The Jewish meeting place for prayer and the reading and teaching of Scripture each Sabbath, found in every town. It began probably during the exile, when the temple lay in ruins. A ruler ran the services and could invite a visitor to read and speak, which is how Jesus and Paul taught there.

column4: law of moses|book of the law|book of moses|law of the lord|book of the covenant|book of the law of moses|the law and the prophets|law and the prophets
column10: God's commands given through Moses at Sinai, written in the first five books of the Bible (the Torah). "The law and the prophets" meant the Scriptures as a whole. Jesus said he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it, and Paul calls it a guardian that leads us to Christ (Gal 3:24).

column9: Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: God told Israel to write his words "upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates". Jews came to keep this by fixing a small case holding these verses (a mezuzah) to the doorframe, and touching it as they went in and out.

column4: phylacteries|phylactery|frontlets|frontals|prayer boxes|scripture boxes|bind them for a sign upon thine hand|between thine eyes|between your eyes
column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: Small leather boxes holding verses of the Law, tied on the forehead and the left arm for prayer, keeping God's command to bind his words "for a sign upon thine hand" and "between thine eyes". Jesus rebuked those who made theirs broad to be seen as holy.

column9: Easton's Bible Dictionary; Edersheim, Sketches of Jewish Social Life
column10: Israelites wore tassels on the four corners of their outer garment, with a blue cord, to remember God's commands. The sick woman touched the "hem" (the tassel) of Jesus' cloak and was healed; some Pharisees made theirs long to look devout.

column4: sackcloth|sackclothes|sack cloth|ashes|dust upon their heads|dust on their heads|dust on his head|dust upon his head
column10: Signs of grief and repentance. Sackcloth was rough cloth of goat's hair, worn next to the skin; mourners sat in ashes or threw dust on their heads. When Nineveh repented, even the king put on sackcloth and sat in ashes.

column4: rent his clothes|rent their clothes|rent her clothes|rent his garments|rent their garments|rent his mantle|rent his robe|rent my garment|tore his clothes|tore their clothes|tore her clothes|tore his robes|tore his robe|tore their robes|tore his garments|tore his cloak|tore their garments|tore my clothes|tear your clothes|rend your clothes|rend your heart|rent his clothing|tore his clothing|tore their clothing
column10: Tearing one's garment at the neck showed great grief, horror or outrage, at news of death or disaster, or at hearing blasphemy, as the high priest did at Jesus' words. Joel calls for something deeper: "rend your heart, and not your garments" (Joel 2:13).

Places of worship, often on hilltops, with an altar and sometimes a sacred pole or stone. The Canaanites worshipped their gods there; Israel too offered sacrifices at high places, at first to the Lord, but they led to idolatry. Good kings like Hezekiah and Josiah tore them down, so worship would be at the temple alone.

column4: asherah|asherim|asherah pole|asherah poles|asheroth|grove|groves|sacred pole|sacred poles|wooden image|wooden images
column10: Wooden poles or carved images set up for Asherah, a Canaanite goddess of fertility, often beside altars to Baal. The King James Version calls them "groves". God commanded Israel to cut them down; Gideon and later reforming kings did.
Small figures kept in homes, thought to bring blessing and sometimes used to seek omens. Rachel stole her father Laban's; Michal used one to fool Saul's men. They are always condemned as idols.

column4: divination|divinations|diviner|diviners|soothsayer|soothsayers|soothsaying|enchanter|enchanters|enchantment|enchantments|sorcerer|sorcerers|sorcery|sorceries|witchcraft|witch|necromancer|medium|mediums|familiar spirit|familiar spirits|wizard|wizards|spiritist|spiritists|fortune-telling|fortune teller|magician|magicians|magic arts|observe times|observer of times
column10: Ways the nations tried to learn the future or gain power from spirits: reading omens, consulting the dead, casting spells and magic. The Law forbade them all as an abomination (Deut 18:9-14): Israel was to listen to God and his prophets. Saul's visit to the medium at Endor was part of his downfall.

column4: sons of the prophets|company of prophets|company of the prophets|band of prophets|group of prophets|guild of prophets|school of the prophets
column10: Groups of prophets who lived and learned together under a leader such as Samuel, Elijah or Elisha. "Sons" here means members or disciples, not children.
